Unpairing and revocation Removing a device in the app deletes its key. Revoking from the host closes that device's link immediately and refuses the next connection — the token it held is spent. Neither touches your bots, your profiles or anything else on the host.

b: HTTPS fails but the bridge is healthy Tailscale issues the certificate on first use; a fresh domain can take a minute. If it persists: tailscale cert <host>.<tailnet>.ts.net curl -v https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net:8443/v1/health Copy

h: The app cannot reach the host
b: The app cannot reach the host Is the device on the tailnet, logged into the same one? Does the URL in the app exactly match hermey pair 's output, including the port? curl https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net:8443/v1/health from another tailnet device — if that fails, the problem is the host, not the app.
A pairing code is rejected Codes are single-use and expire in minutes. Mint a fresh one with hermey pair . Repeated failures are rate limited per client, so wait a moment after a handful of attempts.

h: The iOS app stops launching after a week
b: The iOS app stops launching after a week That is free-Apple-ID signing, not a bug. Re-sign through AltStore or SideStore, or use a paid developer account for a one-year profile.

h: macOS says the app is damaged
b: macOS says the app is damaged The build is unsigned. Right-click → Open the first time, or once: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Hermey.app Copy

Trust boundaries Boundary Crossing it requires What is on the other side Public internet → tailnet Tailscale identity + ACL nothing: no public ingress exists Tailnet → bridge TLS to tailscale serve , then a single-use 30 s ticket pairing, tokens, /v1/ws Bridge → gateway loopback plus the gateway token, which is never s

Invariants The bridge listens on loopback only; tailscale serve is the only front door. Tickets are single-use and expire in 30 seconds; a device is identified by its own Ed25519 key. The device never receives the gateway token — it cannot talk to the agent directly. Approvals are the agent's to ask and the human's to

Deliberately absent No account, no analytics, no crash reporting, no relay of ours in the request path. No public ingress: if the tailnet is up but the device is not on it, nothing is reachable. No per-bot permission system on the Mac. Computer use is one owner-level switch — a small number of trusted bots is the state

Where the apps keep secrets The phone keeps its device key and refresh token in the Keychain, this-device-only. The Mac build ships unsigned and has no Keychain entitlement, so it keeps the same items in a 0600 file under ~/Library/Application Support/Hermey/ , excluded from backups.

The problem A bot asked to "log into my Doctolib account" today has two bad options: be handed the password (it ends up in a transcript, a log and a model's context), or be given standing access to a vault (any bot can then read anything). Neither is acceptable, and both are how automation normally does it.

The idea The bot orchestrates the login. The owner supplies the secret. The two are kept apart: the secret is typed into a card in the Hermey app and flows from the app, through the bridge, into the page. It never enters the conversation, the bot's context, or a log. Every secret-bearing interaction is a card . There a
